# Systems of linear equations (elimination and matrices) (`linear_equations_matrices`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/math.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Mathematics & measurement (`math`)
- Deps: helped by negative_numbers, abacus_counting_board, symbolic_algebra
- Core idea: Several unknowns tied by several conditions are found by elimination: write the coefficients in a rectangular array, multiply rows and subtract them from each other until each row has one unknown fewer, then substitute back. The classic Chinese problem: 3 bundles of good, 2 of medium and 1 of poor grain give 39 measures; 2, 3 and 1 give 34; 1, 2 and 3 give 26; elimination yields 9 1/4, 4 1/4 and 2 3/4 measures per bundle. Treating the array itself as an object (a matrix) with its own multiplication later organises geometry, mechanics and statistics.
- Pitfalls:
  - Calling the method Gauss's invention. It is in the Chinese Nine Chapters about 1,800 years before him.
  - Expecting a unique answer when there are fewer independent conditions than unknowns, or when two conditions contradict each other.
  - Avoiding negative intermediate values, which the method cannot do without.
  - Assuming matrix multiplication is commutative (A times B is generally not B times A).
- History: mesopotamia: c. 1800 BC – two-unknown problems solved by substitution; china: c. 1st c. AD – Nine Chapters, ch. 8 (fangcheng), elimination on the counting board with positive and negative rods; india: 628 – Brahmagupta treats several unknowns with colour names; east_asia: 1683 – Seki Takakazu (Japan) uses determinants; europe: 1693 Leibniz on determinants (unpublished); 1707 Newton, Arithmetica universalis, elimination; 1750 Cramer's rule; 1809–1810 Gauss's notation for least-squares systems; 1858 Cayley, algebra of matrices
- Read:
  - Roger Hart, The Chinese Roots of Linear Algebra (2011)
  - Joseph F. Grcar, How Ordinary Elimination Became Gaussian Elimination, Historia Mathematica 38 (2011)
